reviews.review: This game is interesting, entertaining, and a little challenging. I like the story that it conveys. If you want to get used to using the command line for windows and Unix, this game can help you get use to the basic commands like cd (change directory), ls ( listing contents in current directory for unix), dir (the same as ls but its for windows command line) and etc. The music is amazing to listen to. The visuals are so good to look at. The game gets you that hacker feel. Like you are the ones from the movies. Highly can recommend to friends.
For Terminal Freaks like me, this game is so interesting and adventures and has a nice story to make it more interesting.

Game is an experience unlike any other, if you aren't good at typing you might not enjoy it, but you will enjoy it much more if you do. Had people thinking I was hacking in real life when they came up to me and asked if it was a game. There are times when you might even second guess yourself if what you are doing is illegal or real life. Very immersive 11/10 Workshop/extension support adds many free playthroughs that change the game up and add new features. Cannot recommend enough.

The concept for this game was really great. I was very excited to try it. I am a heavy Linux user and I expected this to be a fun game that would be gamified but have it's roots in the real world. The gamification was too heavy for me. Lots of basic commands that would be used on the command line act completely different. Especially ones that you use to connect and transfer files from one computer to another over the network. It quickly turned into a frustrating experience where I was required to reteach myself completely new paradigms of using programs I have been using for over a decade and I just couldn't handle it.
Had fun investigating around systems over network. More like puzzle game done on command line (finding clues, passwords, IPs etc..) if you are already accustomed to cmd
You better go learning Linux and get a real job as SysOps or DevOps. This will be much more funny than playing this game.

This is an extremely fun game, don't get me wrong, but I have two very major issues with it (especially the second one) that have prompted me to leave a negative review.  I very rarely review games on Steam, and only review the ones about which I am most passionately moved, positively or negatively.  In this case, negatively.  In contrast to my usual, I have enabled comments on this review -- feel free to state your feedback, whether you agree with me or not, just please remain respectful to me, the developers, other commenters, and anyone else as applicable.

There's a "TL;DR" at the end if you're lazy.

I'll start positive.  This game is crazy fun.  It is probably the funnest hacking-themed game I've ever played, and I've played a lot of them.  It was fun and helpful to see some things I recognize from real life, such as the default system port numbers being accurate and the existence of a few UNIX commands (my main OS has been FreeBSD for years, and my experience with UNIX helped with the gameplay in a way that felt good).  I liked seeing the C# source code and realizing it was actual, real C# source code that would probably work if the LESS_THAN was properly changed to a "<" sign, etc (C# is my main dev language, always a plus to see it referenced in a game at all).  That was cool, and I'll probably compile it later to have that tool on my PC for real (don't comment about the related real life security to this -- I assure you I already know, and it's just for fun).  The pacing was really good, and I got hooked fast.  So fast that I immediately bought the DLC, soundtrack, and DLC soundtrack for myself, then bought the game and DLC for both my wife and her boyfriend also.  Despite my negative review, I don't regret this decision at all, it's a very, very fun game.  Oh, the event thing that I can't discuss without giving spoilers, but well, the one where you need to get that thing back, that was super fun!  (Unimportant to the review and a spoiler:) I instinctively [spoiler]jumped to my host and forkbombed, apparently I was supposed to kill his forkbomb instead, oh well... I had already made a backup of that file just in case[/spoiler].  But anyway, the game was extremely fun, looks great, the music is great, and I'm excited to keep playing and see where things take me.

But there are two issues which were severe enough that they prompted me to leave a negative review despite all this.

The first issue isn't so bad and is easily rectified: This game is the pinnacle of Hollywood-style hacking.  It does it very well, and it references real hacking concepts in the game's flavor text and other areas.  Some tools are named the same as real ones, and you will probably learn a few real UNIX system port numbers, but that's about where the realism ends.  Oh, and [b]this wouldn't bother me in the slightest[/b] -- I love Hollywood-style hacking sim games! -- but it clearly says this in the "Features" section in the game's Steam page description, which to me is [u]blatant false advertisement[/u]:

[quote]
Real Hacking
Based on actual UNIX commands, Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it.
[/quote]

If I stated what I consider my qualifications for knowing what constitutes "Hollywood-style" hacking, nobody would believe me, so I won't.  But even if you have never seen either a vtty or Hackers, I feel like anyone looking at the animation for the command called "porthack", god and the command name itself, and how it works, and everything related to the actual process of hacking (kinda the core concept in the entire game)... well I just think it doesn't take an expert to realize it's about as unrealistic as you can get.  If you don't believe me and this matters to you, buy the game and try it.  You will know I'm right within the 2 hour window to return it for a full refund, I assure you.  There is no "SSHCrack", no "FTPBounce", these wouldn't be PE executables if they did exist, PE doesn't even run on UNIX, "opening ports" and having requirements for a certain arbitrary number of open ports to "porthack" is very Hollywood.  Stahp.  Hollywood-style hacking is fine, don't be ashamed of it!  But most importantly, [b]advertise this game for it's many strengths, not for a falsehood[/b].  This game doesn't need lies to make it sound good, it's already a good game.  It's already a [i]great[/i] game.  Don't make false claims that sour its image.

Ok, now for the big one (to me).  Some people, many perhaps, won't care about this but I care.  I am quite literally sick to my stomach right now.  This has perhaps very minor spoilers for a very small number of optional (so far where I am in the story) missions, so I will spoiler-tag a lot to be safe, but even if you haven't played the game and hate spoilers, you probably won't be upset for reading the spoiler-tagged text in the next paragraph, it's the mildest of mild spoilers.

So, some of the missions require you to access a database of [spoiler]death row records[/spoiler] and modify them.  The missions are fine, and the topics are relevant.  I thought this was a positive thing to include in the game... until I gained access to this database and actually started reading the records.  I read about 40 of them in a row, unable to stop.  These were not made up, they were real records.  They had to be.  Surely the names were changed at least, right?  I Googled one at random and sure enough it was entirely real, and even the name, age, and date matched.  The [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] were their real [spoiler]last words[/spoiler], verbatim.  There is literally a massive database of actual real people's [spoiler]deaths[/spoiler] including their real [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] in the game, and there are missions to modify this database!  It is making light of a very serious topic with real people's real, actual names, turning it into a game.  If I am [spoiler]executed[/spoiler], I don't want my [spoiler]last words[/spoiler] to be made into a fun, "cool" game.  That's awful!  These families are mourning!  Please do not take real, actual tragedy and juxtapose it alongside comical IRC chat logs!  In a game?!  If you are a U.S. company, the families of these people may have legal justification to press charges.  I almost hope they do.  But instead of that, I would rather you modify your game and replace the real data with artificial data that you make up, or at least change the names and please also [spoiler]their last words[/spoiler].  This would have been such a cool set of missions, with a positive political message, but since you used real data it ruins the whole thing and instead makes it a mishandled slog of insensitivity... or... words, I just hate that you used real data for this.  Please replace it with artificial data.  It won't hurt the game.  It will take a single developer a day, if that, and then you can be on the right side of things, morally and honestly probably legally.  I plan to ask my lawyer his opinion on this sometime when he's not busy, not to press charges myself (I'm not listed in the data), but just out of legal curiosity if charges could be pressed for something like this.

Anyway this is a fun game and I'm not going to try to refund it, I'm not even going to stop playing it, but I will stop recommending it or buying it for more people (I have a tendency to buy games I like repeatedly for lots and lots of people, friends, family, etc.).  I think I bought Necesse 12 or 13 times?  I also fully plan to modify this review if my issues are addressed.  I will do so as soon as I notice the changes.  If you reply to this review when you've addressed them, I will likely notice faster and therefore update it faster... you know, if you don't want one nerd girl's negative review.

TL;DR: Great game, super fun.  But it uses false advertising on its Steam page, and is horribly insensitive to real mourning families IRL, and doesn't even change the names.

-- Amy

Although it's not like real life hacking which is far more complex and tedious and causes your adrenaline to go up far more (I know since I used to hack with the permission of the lab administrator to find all her security flaws), HackNet is by far and large, the best hacking game I've ever played. I would recommend buying HackNet: Labyrinths as well, because it makes the experience way better and has some extra stuff for you. Plus you get to see what the Labyrinths missions are actually all about in the end. Buying HackNet + HackNet: Labyrinths (I suggest HackNet - Complete Edition since it's cheaper and has both all in one) also allows you access to a variety of extensions (user made mods using the HackNet scripting language), including those that require the HackNet: Labyrinths DLC to play them. All in all an interesting game story-wise and although I find it a bit script kiddie-like, it's still fun to play, since you can actually write some programs of your own to do similar things if you have enough time, patience and skill. In only some cases though. Some things still need to be done manually.

First game of it's kind that I've played.  It's a fun and easy game about reading and following instructions.  The hardest thing in the game is reading carefully.  It loosely following the idea of 'hacking' in a game-ified format.   Most of the terminal commands are the very basic ones.  Some of them don't work the way they're supposed to; cd doesn't take you back to the home directory.  'rm *example*' Doesn't remove files containing "example" in the name with anything before or after it.  'mv' can rename files, but it can't move files outside of the directory it's already in.  This is no 'pwd' and you can't 'touch' files.  You also can't update your imaginary system or check what OS version and kernel it's running.  These are all terrible oversights, each one less relevant than the next.  The point is, you're not going to be expected to do anything more overwhelming than remembering a few words to type.  You'll find using them is more fun than you'd expect.

But alot of these commands are watered down, like no flags to change how some of these commands work, which is very important when you want to do more stuff, I think this is okay for a game though. Something else though to note, is often it is not case sensitive ingame, this is very important in computers though changing the case of a letter makes it a different command or program altogether very often, keep that in mind while you play and just have fun. The truth of the matter is this is a puzzle game, and if you like to think of ways around things, this is the kind of puzzle game you want.

"My First Hacker" is definitely fun to give all those play-pretend hacker vibes. Love the music, too, even if it can be a little repetitive at times. Reason I call it "My First Hacker" is because, from my tiny and incomplete understanding of "Real-World Hacking", the only things you'll see here are a couple of the "ports" (HTTP being 80, for example), and a very general feel of typing stuff out for computer commands...oh, but at least the peoples' usernames you find in-game sound like something I'd expect to come across on the Internet. 

The only real improvement, I wish there were a less thorny way to edit text and in-game documents. It's not like you can open up Notepad and type whatever you want. You have to 1) download a spare copy of any file you find; 2) use the in-game replace or rename functionality, 3) use quotation marks to replace any old words with what you want to fill with. Also keep in mind, 4) the final wording should not be something that shows up elsewhere, so it's easier to append your journal for later - so sign off with a catchphrase of your choosing. Replying to emails is funny since you can say whatever you want to those hackers, and unless it's mission-critical, they'll ignore all that flavor text (but that's just an inherent limitation with computer games being as hardcoded as they are).

And the entire vanilla game is about quarter a gig large (or maybe 1 gig with the entire expansion pack). SO it should fit mostly easily on most any modern hard drive. 

Overall, I like it. It's definitely more of a game than a teaching tool, and that's fine.

Edit: there's just one main criticism, and that is for a 99% text-based game, the text is RIFE WITH TYPOS! Apostrophe abuse ("it's its problem") is EVERYWHERE, and for Colonel's Chicken, the employee welcome letter spells it Kernal (like the computer component instead of the obvious Colonel of the KFC reference).

It feels like a successor to the mechanics in Uplink (See Introversion Software).  This sets itself apart with a story up front.  There's also the benefit of not really worrying about having your progress completely terminated.  While there was a certain charm in learning through brutality, this allows you to make progress and practice your hacks without having to slog through a bunch of earlier levels.That's not to say this game won't give you a shock or throw you for a loop here and there.

Not sure how accessible this game is for the command-line uninitiated, but the fact it allows some real life unix commands for renaming, copying files over a network, removing files makes the experience that much more captivating.  The game also indirectly teaches you a little about how these hacks would actually work, without giving away the secret sauce.  For those who have always wanted to feel like they work among the H/=\Xx0rZ of the planet, you might give this a go.
When they tell you to cover your tracks, that's not just fluff.  What you take, destroy, and leave behind (intentional or not) has narrative consequences.
